name: Complementary eyeshadow for iris color

card.summary: Choosing eyeshadow shades opposite the iris on the color wheel so eye color looks more vivid.

quick.overview:
Complementary eyeshadow means picking shadow colors that contrast with your iris color: warm bronzes and coppers for blue eyes, plums for green, blues and purples for brown.

It is a quick, reversible way to make the eyes the focal point of a face.
quick.mechanism: Colors opposite each other on the color wheel intensify one another when placed side by side, so the shadow makes the neighboring iris look more saturated.
quick.risks: Cosmetic eye products carry the usual risks of irritation or allergic reaction. No studies have measured the effect on perceived attractiveness.

lead: Complementary eyeshadow for iris color is a makeup approach in which shadow shades are chosen from the opposite side of the color wheel to the iris, so the eyes look brighter and more vivid. Practitioners commonly pair warm copper, bronze and terracotta tones with blue eyes, plum, burgundy and bronze with green or hazel eyes, and purple, green or bronze-gold with brown eyes.[3] It is a low-cost, reversible way to make the eyes a focal point of the face without changing the eyes themselves.

Wikipedia describes eye shadow as a cosmetic applied mainly to the eyelids to make the eyes stand out, and says it can complement eye color, add depth and draw attention to the eyes.[1] Makeup brand Jane Iredale's guide explains the principle as picking shades from the opposite side of the color wheel because contrasting hues make eyes stand out, and says shimmery or metallic finishes can echo flecks of color in the iris.[3]

Forum posts about appearance advice mention that surrounding colors can make blue eyes "pop".[2] No published trials have tested whether complementary shades change perceived attractiveness; the idea comes from color theory and makeup-artist practice.

chain: Shadow shade is chosen opposite the iris on the color wheel
Contrast intensifies how saturated the iris looks
Eyes become the focal point of the face
angle.text: A well-chosen shade sits next to the iris and makes its color read as more vivid. Users apply it across the lid, at the outer corner or as liner along the lash line to keep the contrast close to the eye.

paras: The approach starts from the iris color and selects shades that contrast with it. Jane Iredale's guide lists orange-based shades such as rich browns and terracotta for blue eyes, with gold, bronze or champagne shimmer to bring out gold flecks.[3] For green and hazel eyes, red is opposite on the wheel, and the guide suggests pinks or darker reddish tones such as bronze, rust and mahogany, and eggplant shadow, noting pure red can look less natural.[3]

For gray eyes it suggests steely shades such as silver, mink gray or icy blue. It calls brown the most versatile eye color, with deep purple, bronzy gold, mossy green or charcoal among its suggestions.[3] Shadow may be applied across the lid, on the outer corner or as a liner along the lash line, which keeps the contrast close to the iris.

Eye makeup dates to predynastic Egypt, around 5000 to 4000 BCE, where green malachite and black galena paints have been found in burials. Eye shadow became a commercial product in the 1910s in the United States, and Elizabeth Arden introduced it in her salons in 1914. It is most often sold as a powder but also comes in liquid, pencil, cream and mousse forms.[1]

Style discussions on forums treat eye color as a feature to be highlighted with surrounding colors, including hair color and makeup.[2] Such advice is mostly given for women's makeup, though the same color logic is used in cosmetic guides generally.

timeline.event: Elizabeth Arden introduces eye shadow in her salons; it becomes a standard commercial product in the 1910s and 1930s.[1]

lore.intro: Forum participants mention that surrounding colors can make eye color stand out.[2]

claims.believers: Posters say warmer hair and makeup colors make blue eyes stand out more.[2] Makeup brands recommend orange-based browns, terracotta and bronze for blue eyes.[3]
claims.experts: No published studies have tested complementary shadow against perceived eye color or attractiveness.

claims.claim: Shimmer can echo flecks in the iris
claims.believers: Jane Iredale's guide says gold, bronze or champagne shimmer can bring out gold flecks in blue irises.[3]
claims.experts: No published studies have examined this effect.
